learnings.title: Flexbox: Wrapping Children into Equal Thirds
Centering an Element in CSS
learnings.answer:
**Question:** given a parent `<div>` and a child `<div>`, centre the child horizontally and vertically.

## The modern answer

```css
.parent {
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;      /* cross axis  — vertical in a row */
  justify-content: center;  /* main axis   — horizontal in a row */
  height: 300px;            /* the parent needs a height to centre within */
}
```

Two lines. The one thing people forget is that **the parent needs a defined height** — centring vertically inside a container that's only as tall as its content does nothing visible.

Note the axis trap: `align-items` and `justify-content` swap meaning under `flex-direction: column`. Centring both ways looks identical either way, which is why this is a safe default.

## Grid: shorter still

```css
.parent {
  display: grid;
  place-items: center;   /* shorthand for align-items + justify-items */
  height: 300px;
}
```

`place-items: center` is the shortest correct answer in modern CSS. There's also `place-content: center` for centring the whole track, and `margin: auto` on a grid child centres it in both directions.

## Absolute positioning

When the child must be removed from flow — an overlay, a modal, a badge:

```css
.parent { position: relative; height: 300px; }

.child {
  position: absolute;
  top: 50%;
  left: 50%;
  transform: translate(-50%, -50%);
}
```

`top/left: 50%` positions the child's **top-left corner** at the centre, so it sits low and right. `translate(-50%, -50%)` pulls it back by half its own size — and percentages in `transform` resolve against the element itself, which is what makes this work without knowing the child's dimensions.

One caveat worth knowing: `transform` creates a stacking context and a containing block for fixed-position descendants, which can surprise you later ([portals](/advanced-react/13) covers where that bites).

## Comparison

| Method | Use when | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| `flex` + `align/justify: center` | Default choice, content in flow | Parent needs a height |
| `grid` + `place-items: center` | Same, shortest syntax | Same |
| `position: absolute` + `translate` | Child must leave the flow | Creates a stacking context |
| `margin: auto` (flex/grid child) | Single child, no parent alignment | Doesn't work in normal flow vertically |
| `text-align` + `line-height` | Single line of text only | Breaks on wrap; legacy |

## Horizontal only, block element

The classic still works and is still right:

```css
.child { width: 300px; margin: 0 auto; }
```

Needs a defined width — `auto` margins split leftover space, and without a width there's no leftover.

learnings.title: CSS Specificity and Selector Priority
learnings.answer:
**Question:** given some HTML and CSS rules, what colour does the text end up, and how does rearranging the rules change it? *The specific snippet wasn't included, so this works through the algorithm and a representative example you can apply to any version of the question.* ## How the cascade decides When several rules set the same property on the same element, CSS resolves it in this order — each step only consulted if the previous tied: 1. **Origin and importance** — `!important` beats normal declarations 2. **Specificity** — the score below 3. **Source order** — last one wins ## Scoring specificity Count three numbers, `(id, class, type)`, and compare left to right. A higher number in an earlier column wins outright, no matter what follows. | Selector | Score | Notes | |---|---|---| | `p` | 0,0,1 | type / element | | `.text` | 0,1,0 | class | | `[data-x]` | 0,1,0 | attribute — counts as a class | | `:hover` | 0,1,0 | pseudo-class — counts as a class | | `::before` | 0,0,1 | pseudo-**element** — counts as a type | | `#title` | 1,0,0 | id | | `div p` | 0,0,2 | two types | | `.card p` | 0,1,1 | | | `#main .card p` | 1,1,1 | | | `*`, `>`, `+`, `~` | 0,0,0 | combinators add nothing | **A single id beats any number of classes.** `#title` (1,0,0) wins against `.a.b.c.d.e` (0,5,0), because the id column is compared first. Specificity is not a sum. Inline `style=""` sits above all of them, and `!important` above that. ## Worked example ```html

Hi

``` ```css p { color: green; } /* 0,0,1 */ .text { color: blue; } /* 0,1,0 */ .card p { color: red; } /* 0,1,1 */ #box p { color: orange; } /* 1,0,1 */ ``` Result: **orange.** `#box p` scores 1,0,1 and the id column decides it immediately. Remove that rule and it's **red** — `.card p` (0,1,1) beats `.text` (0,1,0) on the type column. Remove that too and it's **blue** — `.text` (0,1,0) beats `p` (0,0,1) on the class column. ## Does rearranging change it? **Only for rules of equal specificity.** Source order is the last tiebreaker, so: ```css .text { color: blue; } .text { color: green; } /* green wins — same specificity, later */ ``` But reordering `p` and `#box p` changes nothing. This is the point of the question: people assume "later wins" is the rule, when it's only the *tiebreaker*. ## The modern pseudo-classes Three that behave differently and come up: - **`:is()`** and **`:not()`** take the specificity of their most specific argument. `:is(#a, p)` scores 1,0,0. - **`:where()`** always contributes **zero**. `:where(#a, p) span` scores just 0,0,1 — ideal for library defaults you want easy to override. ```css :where(.btn) { color: grey; } /* 0,0,0 — any rule beats it */ .btn { color: blue; } /* wins */ ``` ## Practical guidance - **Don't fight specificity with more specificity.** Escalating to `#main .card .text p` makes the next override worse. Flatten instead. - **Avoid `!important`** outside utility classes and third-party overrides. The only way past it is another `!important`, and then you're comparing specificity of important rules. - **Prefer single classes.** A flat class-based system keeps every rule at 0,1,0, where source order is a predictable tiebreaker. That's the core insight behind BEM and utility CSS. ## Related - [Flexbox: Wrapping Children into Equal Thirds](/css/1) · [Centering an Element](/css/2) - [MCQ Hit-List: CSS](/test-prep/19)
